title: Multivariable Chain Rule
body:
The [[Chain Rule]] when a quantity can reach the output by more than one route. One variable gives
you a product of derivatives; several variables give you a **sum of products, one term per path**.

$$
\frac{df}{dt} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}
$$

for $f(x,y)$ with $x = x(t)$ and $y = y(t)$. Read it as: $t$ can affect $f$ through $x$, or through
$y$, so account for both and add.

## The tree diagram

Draw $f$ at the top, its immediate inputs below it, their inputs below those, down to the variable
you are differentiating with respect to. Then:

1. Find **every** downward path from $f$ to $t$
2. **Multiply** the derivatives along each path
3. **Add** the paths together

```
        f
       / \
      x   y            df/dt = (∂f/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂f/∂y)(dy/dt)
       \ /
        t
```

Two paths, two terms. That is the entire rule, and it scales without changing: three intermediate
variables give three terms, and an intermediate variable depending on two independents gives a
partial on the left instead of a total derivative:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}
$$

**Which symbol goes on the left is decided by how many independent variables are left at the
bottom of the tree.** One gives $d$, more than one gives $\partial$. Getting this wrong is the
standard notation slip and it is worth checking every time.

## In gradient form

The whole thing is a [[Dot Product]] once you notice the shape:

$$
\frac{df}{dt} = \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle x(t), y(t)\rangle$ is the path. So the rate at which $f$ changes
along a curve is the [[Gradient]] dotted with the velocity. Two immediate consequences:

- Along a **level curve** $f$ is constant, so the dot product is zero, so **the gradient is
  perpendicular to level curves**. That is the geometric fact [[Lagrange Multipliers]] runs on.
- The change is largest when the velocity points along $\nabla f$, which is why the gradient is the
  direction of steepest ascent rather than merely a convenient bundle of partials.

## Implicit differentiation, for free

If $F(x,y) = 0$ defines $y$ implicitly, differentiate the whole thing with respect to $x$ by the
rule above: $F_x + F_y \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$, so

$$
\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{F_x}{F_y}
$$

which is [[Implicit Differentiation]] from [[CALCULUS 1]] with the bookkeeping done once instead of
per problem.

## Why backpropagation is this note

A [[Neural Network]] is a deep composition, and a weight in an early layer reaches the
[[Loss Function]] through **every** neuron downstream of it. Each of those is a path, so the
derivative of the loss with respect to that weight is a sum of products over all of them, which is
exactly the rule above with a very large tree.

[[Back Propagation]] is the observation that computing those sums naively repeats enormous amounts
of work, and that sweeping backwards from the output reuses each partial result once. It is
dynamic programming applied to this rule: see [[Dynamic Programming]] for the same idea in
[[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]. The maths is a first-year identity; the algorithm is why training is
feasible at all.
